senses: The catawba grape, a cultivar of North American Vitis labrusca.
A light sparkling wine made from this kind of grape.
The catawba rhododendron (Rhododendron catawbiense).
ety: From Catawba catawba (“catalpa tree”). See also catalpa.

senses: A Japanese cedar (Cryptomeria japonica)
Any box or boxlike structure used to induce sweating, such as of hides or tobacco
The room where a scene is reviewed.
The review process that takes place in a sweat box.
examples: Australia Post has been accused of endangering staff with "sweatbox" uniforms and restricting earlier starts to save money.

senses: A kind of modern, large-scale university, open to all, proposed by Clark Kerr in the 1960s.
The removal of registration, especially
The process by which an employee is removed from work registrant status.
An effect that makes a game character weaker; a negative status effect.
ety: From de- + buff (“to make a player or item stronger”).

senses: A stone used to crush whin for use as winter feed for cattle.
Any hard dark-coloured rock.
ety: Possibly corrupted from quern stone, i.e. stone suitable for making querns; or else, from whin + stone.

senses: to make liberal, free.
to become liberal, free.
A variation in color (often applied to Oriental rugs).
ety: Borrowed from Turkish abraş, from Ottoman Turkish آبراش (abraş), from Arabic أَبْرَش (ʔabraš, “dappled, mottled”).

senses: The 'resort' (right) of specific farmers to have their grain ground at a specific mill or, inversely, the right of a mill to that custom.
A right of prosecution and judgement.
The area over which this right was established.
ety: From Middle English sookne, socne (“district held by a socage”), from Old English sōcn (“jurisdiction, prosecution, soke”, literally “act of seeking”), from Proto-West Germanic *sōkni, from Proto-Germanic *sōkniz (“seeking, inquiry”), from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂g-. Akin to Gothic 𐍃𐍉𐌺𐌽𐍃 (sōkns, “controversy”), Old English sacu (“legal case, dispute”), sēcan (“to seek”), Swedish socken (“parish”), Danish sogn (“parish”), Norwegian sokn (“parish”). More at sake, seek, soke. See also Medieval Latin sōca (“right of jurisdiction”), English soke.

senses: US and Oxford British English standard spelling of randomise.
To attack a ground target through the use of aircraft or missiles.
A syrupy reduction of vinegar (or wine) and sugar
ety: Borrowed from French gastrique. Doublet of gastric.

senses: a person who studies or records topography
From which caffeine has been removed (e.g. decaffeinated coffee).
ety: From de- + caffeine + -ated or de- + caffeinated.

senses: A harsher-sounding form of dubstep music, influenced by house music and heavy metal.
The forelock of a horse.
The front seat at the top of a horse-drawn vehicle.
ety: From Middle English fore-top, for-top, equivalent to fore- + top.

senses: Any fish (or other creatures) that are not targeted as a catch but are unintentionally caught, and often discarded back into the sea.
Any person, animal, or thing, captured unintentionally on camera or film.
examples: Some offer him bags of bycatch—fish too small or net-mangled to sell, rays and seahorses few will want, and so on.

senses: of Indo-Trinidadians, the process of assimilation into the dominant Creole culture.
Of the nature or texture of tuff.
A Japanese style of cooking in which thin slices of meat, or fish, seafood, vegetables and noodles are quickly fried on a hotplate.
ety: From Japanese, 鉄板焼き (teppan'yaki), from 鉄板 (teppan, “iron plate”) + 焼き (yaki, “frying; roasting; broiling”).

senses: To perform this skateboarding trick.
A physical exercise performed by bending over, performing a squat thrust, returning to a standing position, and jumping once.
ety: Named after American physiologist Royal Huddleston Burpee.

senses: A style of Puerto Rican music having a highly syncopated rhythm and often satirical lyrics.
A song in this style.
examples: This eclectic group is dedicated to preserving the Puerto Rican traditions of bomba and plena, two drum-focused (and African-derived) forms of traditional dance music.

senses: Oryzias latipes, a small Japanese ricefish, popular for use in aquariums.
a cheese produced in the Valtelline valley in Lombardy
Someone who whispers.
Someone who tells secrets; a gossip.
Someone who has an uncanny ability to control or manipulate a certain thing or person; an expert or guru in a particular field or subject
ety: From whisper + -er. The extended senses were popularized by the film The Horse Whisperer (1998).
examples: Among my coworkers, I'd been developing a reputation as a boss-whisperer, in part due to the success of my unusual negotiation strategy, and as of that week, the unexpected success of the billboard.
These include Steve Davies, The Boring Company CEO, and Omead Afshar, who once led Tesla's Gigafactory in Austin and is nicknamed “the Elon whisperer”.

senses: Capable of being composed (as from multiple constituent or component elements).
A type of leavened cake often drizzled with liquor.
Someone who believes in protecting domestic producers by impeding or limiting the importation of foreign goods and services via actions taken by government.
A linguistic purist.
ety: Borrowed from French protectionniste, equivalent to protection + -ist.
examples: Vance is now a key messenger for Trump’s economic agenda as the administration pursues sweeping new protectionists policies announced on what they deemed “Liberation Day.”

senses: Having deep, narrow sulci, grooves or furrows.
ety: From Latin sulcātus, perfect passive participle of sulcō (“to plough, furrow”).
examples: The infant's ossature, the thin and brindled bones along whose sulcate facets clove old shreds of flesh and cerements of tattered swaddle.

senses: A person employed to litigate, a lawyer skilled in arguing in court.
examples: The Senate voted Tuesday night to confirm Pam Bondi as attorney general, making the tenacious litigator the latest official to help fill out President Donald Trump’s administration.

senses: A chicken reared to be eaten at a few weeks of age.
A Cornish game hen.
A supermotard.
Experiencing distrust, showing distrust, wary, sceptical, suspicious, doubtful.
Causing or giving rise to distrust.
Resembling crape.
Capable of evolving.
That can be drawn out.
examples: First, an evolvable system can respond quickly to change. In other words, a new system satisfying changed requirements is released onto the market quickly.

senses: Something that repels; that which causes repulsion.
Covered with a lattice-like pattern of diagonally interlaced bendlets and bendlets sinister.
examples: The coats of various noble British families were originally fretty, but later 'simplified' to a single fret

senses: A coffee drink with chocolate syrup added, or a serving thereof.
A flavour that combines coffee and chocolate.
A dark brown colour, like that of mocha coffee.
A strong Arabian coffee.
An Abyssinian weight, equivalent to a Troy grain.
ety: From Mocha, Yemen, a port on the Red Sea, from Arabic اَلْمُخَا (al-muḵā), for its role as a major marketplace for coffee during Ottoman rule. The beans often had a chocolaty flavor, hence by extension came to refer to any coffee with a chocolate flavor, or any mixture of coffee and chocolate flavors, notably coffee with chocolate syrup added.
